note_tweet.text:
Every SEO tactic from 2011 just got reprinted as AEO advice.

Rob Hoffman posted 11 steps to get recommended by Meta Muse after it started recommending his client's product, pushing people to sign up, and talking down the client's biggest competitor. Add aria labels. Put pricing in raw HTML. Replace slogans with definitions. Allow the meta-webindexer crawler in robots.txt. Refresh pages every 30 days. None of it is wrong advice. It is the crawlability and accessibility checklist Google rewarded fifteen years ago, pointed at a new reader.

But the checklist is the boring half of this. A general agent recommending one product as the best option, then walking the user to its signup page, is ad inventory wearing research clothes. There is no sponsored label. No auction. No way to bid, no way to know why you lost, no organic column for the ad to sit next to. Google built its ad economy over twenty years partly because paid results were labeled next to organic ones, and an entire body of advertising law exists for paid endorsements pretending to be editorial. The agent answer has neither the label nor the neighbors. The answer is the only result.

Two fights follow. The cheap one is the checklist race everyone is already running: once every competitor ships the aria labels and the raw-HTML pricing and the freshness stamps, the edge decays and recommendations drift back toward whatever the model happens to prefer. The expensive one is definitional: what counts as a paid placement inside an answer, who is allowed to buy one, and what a platform owes the user in disclosure. Muse's recommendations are either editorial or inventory and Meta has not said which. The AEO industry is about to relitigate the paid-search disclosure fight, except this time the ad can be indistinguishable from the answer.

Brands buying the 11-point checklist are buying a head start with a shelf life. The thing worth buying early is a seat in the argument over what disclosure means in an answer that never shows ten blue links.

note_tweet.text:
Google should have won this. Gemini can see your email, your calendar, your photos, your searches, your maps, every video you’ve watched.

Its personal assistant launched in May, has barely been mentioned since, and this month Google started folding it back into the main app and dropping the name.
The assistant that actually feels like it knows you came from Meta.

Muse launched in September and within days it felt more personal than anything else we use day to day. The interesting question is how, because Meta had less of your data to start with, not more.

In our testing, Muse runs a check-in every thirty minutes. It works through a checklist it writes for itself, looks for anything that needs doing, and has a look over what it knows about you while it’s there. Forty-eight check-ins a day, including on days you never open it. TIME has reported that it also rewrites its notes about you hourly and reviews the day’s conversations each night, so by morning it has already recorded what changed.

That rhythm explains most of the feeling. A good human assistant never needs a briefing, because they’ve been paying attention all day and already know where things stand.

Meta borrowed the idea from OpenClaw, which programmers set up for themselves. What Meta did differently was put it in a free app for ordinary people. The equivalents from OpenAI and Google sit behind paid plans.

So the advantage wasn’t more data. It was keeping what it had currently.

Which points at something bigger about how these models are built. More on that next.

#AI #ContextEngineering #AIAssistants

Meta Superintelligence Labs released Muse Spark 1.3 on September 2, 2026, and https://t.co/QPRInngWC8 lists it in its model catalog under the Meta Muse family. It is a proprietary agentic and coding model, available from Meta through Muse Code and the Meta Model API.

𝗟𝗔𝗬𝗘𝗥 𝟮 𝗪𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗗𝗢𝗘𝗦 𝗜𝗧 𝗗𝗢

It is built for longer horizon work: building context with tools, spotting gaps in its plan, retaining what it has learned and finishing open ended goals. It was trained to ask clarifying questions when instructions are ambiguous, to request help when blocked and to confirm before consequential actions. It also tracks several workstreams in a long, interrupted thread without dropping earlier requirements.

𝗟𝗔𝗬𝗘𝗥 𝟯 𝗛𝗢𝗪 𝗗𝗢𝗘𝗦 𝗜𝗧 𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗞

In comparisons run by Meta engineers, the model used about 20 percent fewer tool calls and 25 percent fewer tokens than Muse Spark 1.2, while producing cleaner, less verbose code. It has a 1M token context window and a maximum output of 131,000 tokens. Meta reports stronger resistance to prompt injection and better judgment about irreversible actions.

𝗪𝗛𝗬 𝗜𝗧 𝗠𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗦 𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗪𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘 𝗜𝗧 𝗙𝗜𝗧𝗦

𝗟𝗔𝗬𝗘𝗥 𝟰 𝗪𝗛𝗬 𝗗𝗢𝗘𝗦 𝗜𝗧 𝗠𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥

Agents fail in two ways: by doing too little and by doing too much. A model that asks before acting and uses fewer tokens addresses both. At https://t.co/QPRInngWC8 standard reference prices, Muse Spark 1.3 costs $1.25 per million input tokens, $0.15 for cache reads and $4.25 for output, so efficiency translates directly into lower Credits per task. https://t.co/QPRInngWC8 is also honest about limits: maximum reasoning was used in Meta's published evaluations but was not available to API users at launch, and improved calibration does not guarantee correct or safe autonomous execution, so applications still need approval gates for consequential actions.

𝗟𝗔𝗬𝗘𝗥 𝟱 𝗪𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘 𝗗𝗢𝗘𝗦 𝗜𝗧 𝗙𝗜𝗧

Within TRON, Muse Spark 1.3 is one more engine behind the same key and base URL that serves more than 70 models, reachable by agents that settle in Credits and that top up through channels including Tron. It sits beside Claude Haiku 5.5, launched on October 8 for fast sub agent work, and GPT 6.1 Sol, aimed at deeper engineering tasks, so a builder can assign each job to the model whose strengths fit.

Taken together, the five layers say the same thing from different heights: a release, a behavior, a measurement, a practical benefit and a place in a larger system. The value is in the whole stack, from a lab's design choices to the account balance that pays for them.

https://t.co/QPRInngWC8 will keep placing the newest frontier models within reach of every agent and builder in the TRON ecosystem.
